body.p: This responds to the Non-Final Office Action dated December 21, 2023.
No claims are presently amended. No claims are presently canceled. No claims are presently added. Thus, claims 1-20 remain pending in this application.

Applicant respectfully invites the Examiner to call the undersigned attorney at such time when the Examiner takes up this application for further examination to discuss the references and the distinctions identified below.

Claim 1 was rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claim 12 of U.S. Patent No. 11,207,018. The Examiner is invited to call the undersigned attorney to request a terminal disclaimer at such time when the claims are otherwise found to be in condition for allowance.
Claims 1-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Wells (U.S. 2011/0295347) in view of Webb (U.S. 2007/0060984). Applicant respectfully traverses for at least the following reasons.

Claim 1 recites, among other things, "sensing neural activity in a patient using at least one electrode" and "determining a color output for a user interface based on the sensed neural activity." This is generally illustrated in FIG. 1B (Color Mapping) and FIG. 8. The references, taken alone or in combination, do not determine a color output for a user interfaced based on nerve activity sensed using an electrode, where different colors correspond to different sensed neural activity.
FIG.1BD

The rejection asserts that Wells discloses "determining a color output for a user interface based on the sensed neural activity" citing paragraphs [0095]-[0096]. We respectfully disagree. Wells is directed to optical nerve stimulation and/or simulation of peripheral nerves (e.g., Title, Abstract).

As provided above, claim 1 recites sensing neural activity using at least one electrode and determining a color output for a user interface based on the sensed neural activity. Regarding a user interface, Wells refers to "input device(s) 905 connected through an interface 906 as part of computer system 904 to provide external user or operator input as to the responses that were caused by each combination of stimulation signals" [0147] and does not specifically refer to a corresponding "output device" on which a color output could be produced. Regardless, Wells does not determine a color output for its user interface based on the sensed neural activity (which was sensed using an electrode).

The optical stimulation is not a user interface used to provide an indication of sensed neural activity. The color of the optical stimulation is not adjusted by sensed neural activity, but rather the wavelength of the optical stimulation appears to be set to interface with desired nerves [0079]- [0083]. Further, infrared wavelengths are not visible and would not be used on a user interface to provide an indication of sensed neural activity.

The rejection relies on the nerve-action-potential (NAP) sensors and/or the image sensors 208 that obtain image data for sensing nerve activity using at least one electrode. Applicant respectfully asserts that it is improper to use either the NAP sensors or the image color sensors for the following reasons.

Paragraph [0095] refers to nerve-action-potential (NAP) sensors used to obtain nerve-and- movement-disorder data, and this data is processed to detect movement disorders and drive optical and/or electrical probes that stimulate the midbrain or brainstem to treat the disorder. Although the NAP sensors sense neural activity, there is no indication that the NAP sensors even change the color of the optical stimulation, not to mention a color output of a user interface to provide an indication of sensed neural activity. Rather, the optical stimulation is delivered to treat a movement disorder detected by the NAP sensors.

Paragraph [0096] refers to "color sensors." These color sensors do not use an electrode to sense neural activity. Rather, these color sensors are used to determine a color of an object so that the vision sensation of the color may be simulated by stimulating (optical and/or electrical) the brainstem or midbrain. The simulations provide sensations related to sensory deficits (e.g., [0001], [0093], [0096] "simulated vision sensation"). There is no indication that the color sensors even change the color of the optical stimulation, not to mention a color output of a user interface to provide an indication of sensed neural activity.
Thus, Wells does not sense neural activity in a patient and determine a color output for a user interface based on the sensed neural activity.
The rejection asserts "Wells et al. discloses the claimed invention having a method

comprising sensing neural activity and determining a color output for a user interface based on the sensed neural activity except wherein the color output includes diferent hue values, diferent saturation values or diferent brightness values for different sensed neural activity, i.e. efferent or afferent neural activity. " The assertion of what Wells discloses is incorrect because, as identified above, Wells does not disclose" sensing neural activity using an electrode and determining a color output for a user interface based on the sensed neural activity."

Similar to Wells, Webb is directed to optical stimulation of nerves and other tissue (Title, Abstract). The rejection relies on Webb [0010] and [0075] for the color output having different hue values, different saturation values or different brightness values for different sensed neural activity. More particularly, the rejection asserts that Webb uses light to provide stimulation to one more nerve fibers wherein a digital or video image of a surgery site is displayed and as nerves are being stimulated the image is annotated to provide a record of response in which said image is a color- coded map of nerve function [0010], in which distinguish color features of the tissue is defined a hue, tint and/or brightness [0075].
Light is used to stimulate action potentials (propagated electrical impulse in a nerve)

([0005], [0050], [0051], etc.). However, the observed responses to stimulating is not sensed nerve activity. Rather, the observed responses are observations such as phantom-limb pain [0009], muscle twitches or subject reporting touch sensation, taste sensation or other sensation [0121], moving the

head [0128], finger motor control, arm touch sense, smell, sight ([0133]). These observations are different than sensing neural activity in a patient using at least one electrode. Although neural activity may be involved with pain, sensation, etc., these observations, in and of themselves, are not sensing neural activity. Webb does not show a sensor that senses nerve activity using an electrode.

Webb [0010] indicates that responses are observed when different areas are stimulated, and a color-coded map may be used to record the observations. The color-coded map is not based on sensed neural activity that was sensed using an electrode. Rather, the color-coded map is based on the observed responses (e.g., pain, sense, smell, sight, etc.).
Webb [0074] discusses an embodiment where visible light is added to invisible IR

stimulation light to provide a visible clue where the stimulation light is aimed. Web [0075] indicates that this visible light may be selected to show a visible difference in reflected brightness for different tissues, and thus may be used to distinguish nerve fibers from other tissue, and a vision system may be used to distinguish color features of the tissues (hue, tint, brightness). The reflected visible light off of different tissue is not sensed neural activity.

For at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of the rejection, and reconsideration and allowance of claim 1. Claim 16 includes language similar to the language of claim 1 and is asserted to be in condition for allowance at least for the reasons provided for claim 1. Claims 2-15 depend from claim 1 and are asserted to be in condition for allowance at least for the reasons provided for claim 1. Claims 17-20 depend from claim 16 and are asserted to be in condition for allowance at least for the reasons provided for claim 16.

In the interest of clarity and brevity, every assertion made in the Office Action may not have been equally addressed. Silence regarding any such assertion does not constitute any admission or acquiescence. All rights not exercised in connection with this response, such as the right to challenge or rebut any tacit or explicit characterization of any reference or of any of the present claims or the right to challenge or rebut any asserted factual or legal basis of any of the rejections, are reserved.

It is respectfully submitted that the claims are in condition for allowance, and notification to that effect is earnestly requested. The Examiner is invited to telephone the undersigned at (612) 373-6900 to facilitate prosecution of this application.
